intro.text: Welcome to Privacy Planet. Life here is generally peaceful, and people usually have nothing much to worry about. However, over the last few years, Privacy Planet is becoming less and less private. Investigate the cause for the issue and help the people on the planet.
intro.computer_text: Hello Cyber Hero! We are told that Patrick the Predatorus is keeping something very <v>valuable** that he stole. We need your help to find what he stole and bring it back to us. This journey will be dangerous, be very careful about ANYONE that you meet on Privacy Planet!

quiz-1.message: Use what you learned to Defeat Enemy 1 and help me get back my information!!!

quiz-2.message: Huh looks like an enemy is trying to follow us! Quick let's defeat them with our knowledge!

quiz-3.message: Looks like we have everything we need to finish this planet! Let's defeat the last enemy to get my sensitive data Back!

 As a token of my appreciation, I award you with a cyber hero sensitive data protector certificate.

parts.part_name: Who Should Sensitive Data Be Shared With?

review_lesson.title: Sensitive Data
review_lesson.message: Is private and personal information that belongs to you and should be kept safe. This kind of information is important because it helps identify who you are, where you live, or how someone can contact you.

review_lesson.title: Sensitive Data Continued
review_lesson.message: Sharing your <v>sensitive data** with the wrong people like Patrick could lead to problems, so it's important to know what <v>sensitive data** is and how to protect it.

options.title: People Can Pretend to Be You

review_lesson.title: Pretending to be You
review_lesson.message: If someone knows your birthday or password, they might pretend to be you online. They could send fake messages to your friends or try to get their private information.

review_lesson.title: Pretending to be You Continued
review_lesson.message: That would be upsetting, right? That's why it's important to keep your information private—so others can't use it to cause trouble.

options.title: People Can Use Your Info to Trick Others

review_lesson.title: Tricking Others
review_lesson.message:
Sometimes, people use your information to trick others.
This is called <v>phishing**, and it's when someone pretends to be you to get private information from your friends or family.

review_lesson.title: Tricking Others Continued
review_lesson.message: They might send fake emails or messages that look real but are meant to steal information. Be careful who you share your information with.

options.title: Who Can You Trust With Your Sensitive Data?

review_lesson.title: Who Can You Trust With Your Sensitive Data?
review_lesson.message: Not everyone should have your <v>sensitive data**. In fact, the less you share, the safer you are. Only certain <v>trustworthy** adults should have access—and only when it's truly necessary.

review_lesson.title: Who Can You Trust With Your Sensitive Data Continued
review_lesson.message:
You can trust:
 <li>Parents or <v>Guardian**s <li>Teachers or School Staff <li>Doctors and Nurses** 
If something feels too personal, talk to your parents right away.

options.title: Who Shouldn't Have Your Sensitive Data?

review_lesson.title: Who Shouldn't Have Your Sensitive Data?
review_lesson.message: Just because someone asks for your information doesn't mean you should give it. Some people pretend to be friendly to trick you.

review_lesson.title: Who Shouldn't Have Your Sensitive Data Continued
review_lesson.message:
Don't give your <v>sensitive data** to:
<li>Strangers<ul>People online<ul>Friends (when it comes to passwords)**
When in doubt, ask or alert a <v>trustworthy** adult if someone asks for your <v>sensitive data**

message.text:
Full Name:

While it's okay to share just your name with people, your full name (first, middle, and last) is special and should be kept private.

Why? Because if a stranger knows your full name, they can look up more information about you, like where you live or where you go to school.

Home Address:

Your home is your safe place, and only trusted people (like family and close friends) should know where you live.

Sharing your address with strangers or online could be dangerous because it tells people exactly where to find you.

Birthday:

Your birthday might seem like a fun thing to share—after all, everyone loves birthday parties!

But did you know that some people can use your birthdate to guess passwords or pretend to be you? Some websites even use your birthday to confirm your <v>identity**, so sharing it could make it easier for someone to pretend they're you online.

Phone Number and Email Address:

Your phone number and email is how people can contact you, and it should only be given to trusted adults, family members, or close friends. 

If a stranger gets your phone number or email, they could call or message you, even if you don't want them to.

There are many things that people may ask you, but you should not tell everyone about everything. Some information is private and personal and should be kept safe. These are all <v>sensitive data**, they can help identify who you are, where you live, and how to find you.
message.speaker: Allie

He could even use your name to send messages to your friends, asking them for private information or trying to trick them into sharing things they shouldn't.
message.speaker: Enemy #2

message.speaker: Allie

message.text: Sometimes, we use <v>sensitive data** to trick other people into giving away more private information. This is called <v>phishing**. Let's say someone gets access to your email address and sends a message to a friend pretending to be you. If your friend isn't careful, they might believe the message and share their personal details. This can cause harm not just to you but to your friends and family, too. HAHAHA!

message.text: Not everyone should have access to your <v>sensitive data**. In fact, most of the time, the less you share, the safer you are! Only certain trusted people should know your personal information, and even then, it should only be shared when necessary.
message.speaker: Allie

message.text: There are a few people who might need to know your personal information, but they should always be adults you trust.
message.speaker: Allie

message.text:
Parents / <v>Guardian**s

Your parents or <v>guardian**s are the most important people to share <v>sensitive data** with because they are responsible for keeping you safe. They can decide when and how your information should be shared. If someone asks for your personal details, always check with your parents first!

Teachers / School Staff

Sometimes, you might need to share certain details with teachers or school staff, like your name or <v>emergency** contact information. However, this should only happen if your parents approve. A teacher will never ask for things like your passwords or private accounts, so if someone at school asks for something that feels too personal, talk to your parents right away.

Doctors / Nurses

Your health information is private, but medical professionals may need to know things like your birth date, allergies, or medical history to take care of you. This is one of the few times when sharing personal details is okay — but only with trusted doctors or nurses, and only when your parents say it's necessary.
However, even if someone seems nice, that doesn't mean you should trust them with your personal information. Some people pretend to be friendly just to get you to share details about yourself.
message.speaker: Allie

message.text:
Strangers:

You should never give <v>sensitive data** to strangers.

If you wouldn't walk up to a random person in a store and tell them where you live, you shouldn't do it online either! People you don't know should never have your personal details, even if they seem friendly.

People Online:

You should never give <v>sensitive data** to people online.

Some people on the internet pretend to be kids or act nice to trick others into sharing information. They might ask things like, “Where do you live?” or “What’s your phone number?” but you should never answer these questions online. If someone asks, tell a parent immediately.

Friends (passwords)

Even if you trust your best friend, never share your passwords — not even for games! They can accidentally share it with the wrong person. Also, if you ever have a fight, they might use it in a way that you don't want.
There are only a few people who might need to know your personal information, and they should always be adults you trust.
message.speaker: Allie
